newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Austria c.bank downplays fiscal EMU criteria.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Austria c.bank downplays fiscal EMU criteria.

text.p: Austrian central bank director Adolf Wala said on Tuesday fiscal entry criteria for Europe's planned single currency were secondary to keeping budget deficits under control over time.

"What is essential is a sustainable budget deficit. This means 3.2 percent with a certain sustainability is better than 2.9 percent with some dirty tricks," he told reporters during a banking conference.
Wala added the essential criteria for Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) were inflation, exchange rate stability and short as well as long term interest rates.
"They influence the stability of the euro. Fiscal criteria are not so important," he said.

Wala's remarks came just a week after a top Austrian government official, state secretary of finance Wolfgang Ruttenstorfer, said employment and growth were more important than rigorous adherence to the entry criteria for EMU.

The Maastricht treaty on EMU stipulates a range of economic targets for countries wanting to join the single currency, including limiting budget deficits to a target three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and public debt to 60 percent.

Austria's softening line on the criteria could set it on a potential collision course with its mighty German neighbour, one of the most vociferous advocates of a strict definition of the entry thresholds.

The debate about how narrowly the criteria should be interpreted has gathered pace over the past few months amid fears that Germany may miss the three percent mark this year, fuelling speculation about a possible delay of EMU.
German participation is seen as a key condition for the project's viability.
Top German officials, eager to convince a sceptical public that the euro will be as hard as the mark, have time and again reaffirmed their commitment to a strict adherence to the criteria.
The Bundesbank, traditionally the anchor of monetary stability in Europe, has also voiced strong objection to any watering down of the EMU criteria or a delay of the project.

Austria itself maintains it will be among the first group of nations to make the race for early admission to EMU, even though its debt-to-GDP ratio is expected to overshoot the 60 percent mark by anywhere up to nine percent.

But in another sign of potential conflict with its EU partners, the Austrian central bank also appears to strongly back early EMU membership of Italy, its second biggest trading partner after Germany.
"My prognosis is that Italy will be part of monetary union in the first stage," Wala said. "If Italy fulfils the criteria we would not hesitate to accept the accession of Italy."

EU finance ministers, issuing a harsh review of Rome's budget situation, on Tuesday urged Italy to get tough on its deficit, saying a further reduction to well below three percent was "necessary to secure a durable budgetary adjustment."
